title: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
summary: How VQ-VAE, VQGAN, FSQ, LFQ and TiTok turn images into short sequences of integer ids: nearest-code quantization, straight-through gradients, codebook collapse, and the bits-per-image budget.
outcomes: Quantize encoder vectors against a codebook and compute the VQ-VAE codebook and commitment loss terms
Explain the straight-through estimator and why codebook vectors need a separate loss or EMA update
Measure codebook usage and perplexity and choose a fix for codebook collapse
Compute FSQ and LFQ codes and token ids and explain why they need no learned codebook
Compute bits per image and compression ratio for a tokenizer and reason about token count versus vocabulary

lessons.title: Why a transformer wants an image as a few discrete tokens

blocks.md:
A language model reads a sequence of integers from a fixed vocabulary and predicts the next one. You already know how BPE builds that vocabulary for text. Can the same model read and *write* images?

The naive answer is to treat every pixel channel as a token. A 256 x 256 RGB image is 256 x 256 x 3 = **196,608 bytes**, so that would be a sequence of 196,608 tokens over a vocabulary of 256 byte values. Self-attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, and most of those values are redundant: neighbouring pixels are strongly correlated.

A **visual tokenizer** fixes this with three learned parts:

1. An **encoder** (a CNN or a ViT) that downsamples the image into a small grid or list of feature vectors.
2. A **quantizer** that replaces each vector with one entry of a finite set, so the image becomes a short list of integer ids, the *visual tokens*.
3. A **decoder** that turns the ids back into pixels.

The encoder and decoder are trained together as an autoencoder. After that, a transformer is trained on the token ids exactly as it would be on text ids, and generated ids go through the decoder to become an image.

blocks.title: Two stages: learn the tokenizer, then model the tokens

scenes.caption: Stage 1 starts with an image. The encoder shrinks each side by a factor f. With f = 16 a 256 x 256 image becomes a 16 x 16 grid of feature vectors.
The quantizer swaps each feature vector for the id of its closest entry in a finite codebook. The image is now 256 integers, like a 256-token sentence.
The decoder maps the ids back to pixels. Reconstruction losses train encoder, quantizer and decoder together so the ids keep what matters.
Stage 2 freezes the tokenizer. A transformer learns the distribution of id sequences. To generate, it samples ids and the frozen decoder renders them.

blocks.md:
This two-stage recipe was introduced by **VQ-VAE** (van den Oord, Vinyals and Kavukcuoglu, 2017), which compressed 128 x 128 x 3 ImageNet images into a 32 x 32 grid of ids from a codebook of K = 512 entries. The paper computes the reduction in bits as $\frac{128 \cdot 128 \cdot 3 \cdot 8}{32 \cdot 32 \cdot 9} \approx 42.6$, since each id needs $\log_2 512 = 9$ bits. A PixelCNN prior was then trained on the ids instead of the pixels.

VQGAN (Esser, Rombach and Ommer, 2021) pushed this to 16 x 16 = 256 tokens for a 256 x 256 image and replaced the PixelCNN with a GPT-2 style transformer.

A visual tokenizer is to images what BPE is to text: a fixed map from raw input to a short sequence of ids from a finite vocabulary. Unlike BPE it is a learned, lossy neural network, so its reconstruction quality caps how good generated images can look.

blocks.prompt: Why not skip quantization and give the transformer the 256 continuous feature vectors directly?
blocks.reveal: You can for *understanding* (many vision-language models do this), but a model that should *generate* images with the same next-token cross-entropy loss it uses for text needs a finite set of outcomes to put a softmax over. Discrete ids give a categorical distribution per position, the same loss and sampling code as text, and one shared vocabulary in which image and text tokens can be interleaved.

blocks.question: A tokenizer downsamples 256 x 256 images by f = 8 instead of f = 16. How long is the token sequence the transformer must model?
options: 256 tokens, because the codebook size is unchanged
1024 tokens, a 32 x 32 grid
512 tokens, because halving f doubles the length
65,536 tokens, one per pixel
blocks.explain: Each side shrinks by f, so the grid is (256/8) x (256/8) = 32 x 32 = 1024 tokens. Halving f doubles each side and therefore quadruples the token count, and the number of attention pairs grows 16x.

blocks.question: What does the transformer in stage 2 actually see as input?
options: Raw RGB pixel values
The encoder's continuous feature vectors
Integer codebook ids, embedded through its own embedding table
The decoder's reconstructed image
blocks.explain: After stage 1 the image is represented only by integer ids. The transformer embeds them with its own learned table and predicts a categorical distribution over the next id, exactly as for text tokens.

lessons.title: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code

blocks.md: The VQ-VAE quantizer keeps a **codebook**: K learned vectors $e_1, \dots, e_K$, each with the same dimension D as an encoder output. For each encoder output $z_e(x)$ it finds the nearest code by Euclidean distance and passes that code to the decoder. The id k is the token.

blocks.caption: Equation 2 of VQ-VAE. The id k is what the transformer later models; z_q is what the decoder receives.

blocks.md:
A toy example. Take a codebook of 6 codes in 2D:

- $e_0 = (1, 1)$, $e_1 = (-1, 1)$, $e_2 = (-1, -1)$, $e_3 = (1, -1)$, $e_4 = (3, 3)$, $e_5 = (0, -3)$

and 4 encoder outputs (think of 4 positions in a tiny 2 x 2 grid):

- $z_0 = (0.8, 1.3)$, $z_1 = (1.4, 0.6)$, $z_2 = (-0.7, 1.1)$, $z_3 = (1.2, -0.5)$

The matrix below holds every squared distance $\lVert z_i - e_j \rVert^2$, computed with numpy.

blocks.title: Squared distances from 4 encoder outputs to 6 codes

scenes.caption: Row i holds the squared distance from z_i to every code. For z0 = (0.8, 1.3), the distance to e0 = (1, 1) is 0.2 squared plus 0.3 squared = 0.13.
Each row picks its minimum. z0 and z1 both land on e0, z2 on e1 and z3 on e3. The token ids for this 2 x 2 image are [0, 0, 1, 3].
Columns e2, e4 and e5 win no row. Those codes get no updates from this batch. If that persists over training they become dead codes, the subject of the next lesson.
The winning distances 0.13, 0.32, 0.10 and 0.29 are the quantization errors. Their mean, 0.21, is what the codebook and commitment losses below are built from.

blocks.md: **The gradient problem.** The argmin has no useful gradient: nudging $z_e$ slightly usually does not change k at all, and when it does, the output jumps. VQ-VAE uses a **straight-through estimator**: in the forward pass the decoder receives $z_q$; in the backward pass the gradient arriving at $z_q$ is copied unchanged onto $z_e$. In code this is one line, `z_q_st = z + stop_gradient(z_q - z)`: its value equals `z_q`, but its gradient with respect to `z` is the identity.

Because of that copy, the codebook vectors receive **no gradient from the reconstruction loss**. VQ-VAE therefore adds two more terms, using the stop-gradient operator sg (identity forward, zero gradient backward):

- The **codebook loss** $\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e \rVert^2$ pulls the chosen code toward the encoder output. Only the codebook learns from it.
- The **commitment loss** $\beta \lVert z_e - \mathrm{sg}[e] \rVert^2$ pulls the encoder output toward its chosen code, so the encoder commits to a code and its outputs cannot grow without bound. Only the encoder learns from it.

blocks.caption: VQ-VAE equation 3, written as a loss to minimise. The paper uses beta = 0.25 in all experiments and reports results did not vary for beta from 0.1 to 2.0.

blocks.title: One VQ forward pass on the toy batch
blocks.code:
z  = encoder(x)                       # (4, 2)
d  = ((z[:, None] - E[None])**2).sum(-1)  # (4, 6)
k  = d.argmin(1)                      # token ids
zq = E[k]                             # chosen codes
cb_loss  = ((sg(z) - zq)**2).sum(-1).mean()
com_loss = ((z - sg(zq))**2).sum(-1).mean()
zq_st = z + sg(zq - z)                # straight-through
x_hat = decoder(zq_st)
loss = recon(x, x_hat) + cb_loss + 0.25 * com_loss

scenes.caption: The encoder emits 4 vectors of dimension 2 for a 2 x 2 latent grid.
All 4 x 6 squared distances at once, the matrix from the figure above.
Argmin per row gives the tokens; indexing the codebook gives the vectors the decoder will see.
Both terms use the same squared errors, averaged over the 4 positions, so in the forward pass the codebook term is 0.21 and the commitment term is 0.21 before beta.
The straight-through line: forward value equals zq, backward gradient flows to z as if quantization were the identity.
Total VQ part of the loss is 0.21 + 0.0525 = 0.2625, added to whatever reconstruction loss the decoder produces.

blocks.prompt: In the toy batch the codebook term and the unweighted commitment term are both 0.21. If they have the same value, why keep two terms instead of one?
blocks.reveal: Their **values** are equal but their **gradients** go to different places. The stop-gradients route the codebook term only into the codes and the commitment term only into the encoder. With beta = 0.25, the codes move toward the encoder outputs four times more strongly than the encoder moves toward the codes, which lets the codebook track the encoder without the encoder output drifting freely.

blocks.md: A common misreading is that the straight-through estimator makes quantization differentiable. It does not: it substitutes the identity gradient. The encoder is updated as if the decoder had received $z_e$, which is a useful but biased approximation that is better when $z_e$ stays close to its code.

blocks.question: In the VQ-VAE loss, which parameters receive gradient from the middle term $\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e \rVert^2$?
options: The encoder only
The decoder only
Both the encoder and the codebook
The codebook only
blocks.explain: sg blocks the gradient to z_e, so only the codebook vectors e are updated by this term. The paper states: the decoder optimises the first term, the encoder the first and last, and the embeddings the middle term.

blocks.question: A new encoder output is z = (0.1, -2.2). Using the toy codebook, which token id does it get?
blocks.explain: Squared distances: e5 gives 0.01 + 0.64 = 0.65, e3 gives 0.81 + 1.44 = 2.25 and e2 gives 1.21 + 1.44 = 2.65. The far-away code e5 wins, and that is exactly how a dead code can come back to life: an encoder output has to land near it.

lessons.title: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes

blocks.md: A codebook only learns where encoder outputs land. A code that is never the nearest neighbour gets no codebook-loss gradient, so it stays where it was initialised and keeps losing. Over training many codes can end up unused. The Jukebox paper (Dhariwal et al., 2020) describes this **codebook collapse**: all encodings get mapped to one or a few vectors while the others go unused, which reduces the information capacity of the bottleneck.

Two simple diagnostics, both computed from how often each code is chosen over a batch:

- **Usage**: the fraction of codes chosen at least once.
- **Perplexity**: $\exp(H)$ where $H = -\sum_k p_k \ln p_k$ is the entropy of the code-frequency distribution $p$. It reads as the effective number of equally used codes. DeepMind's Sonnet VQ-VAE module reports exactly this quantity.

In the toy batch the ids were [0, 0, 1, 3], so $p = (0.5, 0.25, 0, 0.25, 0, 0)$.

blocks.caption: Perplexity 2.83 out of a possible 6. Usage is 3 of 6 codes = 50 percent.

blocks.title: How often each code is chosen in the toy batch

scenes.caption: Before any fix: e0 takes 2 of 4 positions, e1 and e3 one each. e2, e4 and e5 are unused. Perplexity 2.83, usage 50 percent.
Random restart in the Jukebox style: dead code e4 is reset to an encoder output from the batch, here z1 = (1.4, 0.6).
Re-quantize: z1 now sits exactly on e4, while z0 still prefers e0 (0.13 vs 0.85). Counts become 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0. Perplexity rises to 4.0 and the mean quantization error drops from 0.21 to 0.13.

blocks.md:
Fixes used in practice, each from its own paper:

- **EMA codebook updates** (VQ-VAE appendix A.1). Replace the codebook loss with an online k-means: each code moves to the running average of the encoder outputs assigned to it, using decay $\gamma$ (the paper found 0.99 works well). In the toy batch the k-means target for $e_0$ is the mean of $z_0$ and $z_1$, which is (1.1, 0.95).
- **Random restarts** (Jukebox): when a code's mean usage falls below a threshold, reset it to a random encoder output from the current batch.
- **Factorized and l2-normalized codes** (ViT-VQGAN, Yu et al., 2022): look up codes in a low-dimensional space (for example 32-d or 8-d instead of 768-d) and normalise both codes and encoder outputs to unit length, so distance becomes cosine similarity. The authors report this immediately boosts codebook usage, even with 8192 codes.

blocks.tex: N_i^{(t)} = \gamma N_i^{(t-1)} + (1-\gamma)\, n_i^{(t)}, \quad m_i^{(t)} = \gamma m_i^{(t-1)} + (1-\gamma) \sum_j z_{i,j}^{(t)}, \quad e_i^{(t)} = \frac{m_i^{(t)}}{N_i^{(t)}}
blocks.caption: EMA update from the VQ-VAE appendix: n_i is how many outputs chose code i in this minibatch, z_ij are those outputs.

blocks.prompt: Will EMA updates by themselves revive the dead codes e2, e4 and e5 in the toy example?
blocks.reveal: No. EMA moves a code toward the outputs **assigned to it**. A code with $n_i = 0$ step after step has $N_i$ decaying toward zero and never moves toward the data. EMA makes assigned codes track the encoder smoothly, but reviving dead codes needs something extra, such as a restart, a different initialisation, or a quantizer where every code is used by design (next lessons).

blocks.md: Bigger codebooks do not automatically mean more capacity. FSQ (Mentzer et al., 2023) found that VQ's reconstruction FID was best at about 2^11 codes and then stopped improving, at the same point where VQ's codebook usage began to drop, despite an entropy regulariser.
Track usage and perplexity during tokenizer training. A 16,384-entry codebook with perplexity 500 behaves like a much smaller vocabulary and wastes embedding rows in every downstream model.

blocks.question: A tokenizer with 1024 codes reports perplexity 1000 on one batch and 40 on another batch of the same size. What does that tell you?
options: The second batch's images use far fewer distinct codes, or a few codes dominate
The second batch had higher reconstruction quality
Perplexity is the cross-entropy of the transformer, so the second model is better
Nothing; perplexity is always equal to the codebook size
blocks.explain: Perplexity exp(H) of the code-frequency distribution is the effective number of equally used codes. 40 means the batch's tokens concentrate on roughly 40 codes' worth of entropy, which could be simple images or a collapsing codebook; compare across batches to tell which.

blocks.question: Why does a dead code stay dead under the plain VQ-VAE codebook loss?
options: Its gradient is clipped by the commitment term
It receives gradient only when it is the nearest code to some encoder output, which it never is
The straight-through estimator sends it the wrong sign
Its distance is always zero
blocks.explain: The codebook term only involves the chosen code e_k. A code that never wins the argmin gets zero gradient, so it never moves toward the data and keeps losing.

lessons.title: VQGAN: perceptual and adversarial losses for 256-token images

blocks.md: A VQ-VAE trained with a pixel L2 loss gives blurry reconstructions when compressed hard, because averaging plausible details minimises squared error. That was tolerable at 32 x 32 tokens for 128 x 128 images, but a transformer can only afford short sequences. VQGAN's authors chose sequences of 16 x 16 = 256 tokens because that was the maximum feasible length to train a GPT-2 medium model (307M parameters) on a GPU with 12 GB of memory.

To keep detail at that compression, **VQGAN** (Taming Transformers, Esser, Rombach and Ommer) changes the stage 1 training objective:

- The L2 pixel loss is replaced by a **perceptual loss**: the distance between deep features of the original and the reconstruction, which penalises missing texture and edges rather than small colour shifts.
- A **patch-based discriminator** D is trained to tell real images from reconstructions, and the autoencoder is trained to fool it (an **adversarial loss**), which pushes reconstructions toward sharp, realistic textures.
- The quantizer and its codebook and commitment terms stay as in VQ-VAE, with the straight-through estimator.

blocks.caption: VQGAN equations 6 and 7. The adaptive weight lambda compares gradient norms of the two losses at the decoder's last layer G_L; delta = 1e-6 is for numerical stability.

blocks.md:
The **adaptive weight** $\lambda$ balances the two losses automatically. If the adversarial gradient at the last decoder layer is large relative to the reconstruction gradient, $\lambda$ shrinks, and vice versa, so neither loss swamps the other without hand tuning.

VQGAN also adds a single attention layer at the lowest resolution so each code can draw on context from the whole image. A downsampling factor of f = 16 with |Z| = 1024 codes was the usual setting in the paper.

scenes.caption: The autoencoder path: encode, quantize, decode. This is the VQ-VAE core with a stronger CNN and one attention layer at the lowest resolution.
The VQ terms still train the codebook and keep the encoder committed to its codes.
Perceptual loss replaces pixel L2: reconstruction and original are compared in a deep feature space, so blur that keeps pixel error low is still penalised.
A patch discriminator judges local patches as real or reconstructed. Its loss is scaled by lambda, set from the ratio of gradient norms at the decoder's last layer.

blocks.md: Did it work? VQGAN's Table 5 reports **reconstruction FID** on ImageNet validation (FID measures how far the statistics of a set of images are from real images; lower is better). A tokenizer's reconstruction FID bounds what the stage 2 generator can reach, since every generated image passes through the same decoder.

blocks.title: ImageNet reconstruction FID (validation) from the VQGAN paper

scenes.caption: DALL-E's discrete VAE, trained without perceptual or adversarial losses, uses 1024 tokens and scores 32.01. VQGAN with only 256 tokens and 1024 codes scores 7.94.
More capacity helps: a 16,384-entry codebook at 256 tokens reaches 4.98, and 1024 tokens with 8192 codes reaches 1.49 (that variant used Gumbel-softmax quantization).

blocks.md: Reconstruction quality is not the same as generation quality. A larger codebook or more tokens improves reconstruction, but it also makes the stage 2 model's job harder: more classes per softmax and longer sequences. MAGVIT-v2 (next lesson) shows generation FID with a VQ tokenizer getting worse as the vocabulary grows past a point.

blocks.question: A VQGAN's adversarial loss starts dominating training and reconstructions drift away from the input. Which part of the method is designed to prevent this?
options: The commitment loss weight beta
The straight-through estimator
The adaptive weight lambda, computed from gradient norms at the last decoder layer
The sliding attention window used at sampling time
blocks.explain: lambda = grad of L_rec / (grad of L_GAN + delta) at the last decoder layer. When the GAN gradient grows relative to the reconstruction gradient, lambda falls, scaling the adversarial term down.

blocks.question: Why did the VQGAN paper target 256 tokens per image rather than, say, 1024?
options: The codebook had only 256 entries
256 was the longest sequence they could feasibly train a 307M GPT-2 medium on with a 12 GB GPU
The perceptual loss only works on 16 x 16 grids
Longer sequences always give worse reconstructions
blocks.explain: The paper states 16 x 16 was the maximum feasible length for GPT-2 medium on a 12 GB GPU. The perceptual and adversarial losses were what made reconstructions at that strong compression good enough.

lessons.title: FSQ and LFQ: quantizers with no learned codebook

blocks.md: Lesson 3 showed that learned codebooks need care to stay fully used. Two later methods remove the learned codebook entirely: the set of codes is fixed by construction, every code is reachable, and the codebook loss disappears.

**Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ)** (Mentzer, Minnen, Agustsson and Tschannen, 2023) projects the encoder output down to a few dimensions, typically fewer than 10. Each dimension i is squashed into a bounded range and **rounded to one of $L_i$ integer levels**. The codebook is implicit: every combination of levels, so $|C| = \prod_i L_i$. Rounding uses the same straight-through trick: `round_ste(x) = x + sg(round(x) - x)`.

The paper recommends levels per target size, for example [8, 6, 5] for about $2^8$, **[8, 5, 5, 5] for about $2^{10}$** (8 x 5 x 5 x 5 = 1000 codes), and [8, 8, 8, 5, 5, 5] for about $2^{16}$, with the heuristic $L_i \ge 5$.

blocks.tex: \hat z_i = \mathrm{round}\big( \tanh(z_i + s_i) \cdot h_i - o_i \big), \qquad h_i = \tfrac{(L_i - 1)(1 - \epsilon)}{2}, \; o_i = \begin{cases} 0.5 & L_i \text{ even} \\ 0 & L_i \text{ odd} \end{cases}, \; s_i = \tan(o_i / h_i)
blocks.caption: The bound function from the FSQ paper's reference code (eps = 1e-3). Even L needs the half-step offset so that exactly L integers are reachable.

blocks.title: FSQ with levels [8, 5, 5, 5] on one vector

scenes.caption: A 4-dimensional encoder output and the per-dimension level counts. The implicit codebook has 8 x 5 x 5 x 5 = 1000 entries; nothing is stored or learned.
Bound each entry. Dimension 0 (L = 8) maps into about (-4.0, 3.0); the others (L = 5) into about (-2.0, 2.0). The tanh keeps -2.5 from running off the end.
Round to integers: 3, -1, 1, -2. Dimension 0 can take the 8 values -4 to 3, the others the 5 values -2 to 2.
Divide by half the level count (4, 2, 2, 2) to rescale into [-1, 1]. This vector goes to the decoder.
Token id: shift levels to digits 7, 1, 3, 0 and read them in mixed radix with place values 1, 8, 40, 200. Id = 7 + 8 + 120 + 0 = 135, one of 1000.

blocks.md: FSQ reports codebook usage near 100 percent for most models with no auxiliary losses: no codebook loss, no commitment loss, no restarts. Because the codes form a fixed grid in a bounded box, the encoder can reach every cell and there is nothing for a code to fall behind on. In the paper's MaskGIT experiments FSQ uses almost all codes even at $2^{14}$ = 16k, where VQ's usage drops. At small codebook sizes VQ was marginally better, which the authors attribute to VQ's more expressive learned code positions.

**Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ)** comes from MAGVIT-v2 (Yu et al., *Language Model Beats Diffusion: Tokenizer is Key to Visual Generation*). It takes the idea to the extreme: each of $\log_2 K$ dimensions has just two values, $\{-1, 1\}$, so quantization is the sign function and the index is the binary number formed by the positive dimensions.

blocks.caption: MAGVIT-v2 equations 3 and 4. No distance computation and no codebook lookup, hence lookup-free.

blocks.title: LFQ on a 4-dimensional vector: K = 2^4 = 16 codes

scenes.caption: Four latent dimensions give 2^4 = 16 possible tokens. MAGVIT-v2 uses 18 dimensions for a vocabulary of 2^18 = 262,144.
Quantize each dimension to its sign. Note 0.1 becomes +1 just like 0.7: LFQ keeps only which side of zero each value is on.
Positive dimensions are 1-bits. Index = 1 x 1 + 4 x 1 = 5. The squared quantization error here is 1.43; the commitment loss pulls encoder outputs toward plus or minus 1.

blocks.md: Because every token is just a sign pattern, LFQ needs no codebook loss. To keep all codes in use, MAGVIT-v2 adds an **entropy penalty** $E[H(q(z))] - H[E(q(z))]$: low entropy per sample (each output confidently picks one code) and high entropy of the batch-average (all codes get used). It is trained with reconstruction, GAN, perceptual and commitment losses as in VQGAN. The paper shows that with LFQ both reconstruction and generation FID keep improving as the vocabulary grows, while with VQ generation quality worsens at large vocabularies.

FSQ and LFQ trade a learned codebook for a fixed grid. You lose the freedom to place codes where the data is dense, and gain full usage by construction, no codebook loss, and vocabularies of 2^16 to 2^18 that VQ struggles to use.

blocks.prompt: FSQ uses levels [8, 5, 5, 5]. You switch to [8, 5, 5, 5, 5] for the next model. What happens to the codebook size and the bits per token?
blocks.reveal: The codebook grows from 1000 to 5000 entries, and bits per token grow from $\log_2 1000 \approx 9.97$ to $\log_2 5000 \approx 12.29$. Adding a dimension multiplies the implicit codebook by that dimension's level count; nothing new is learned, but the stage 2 model now needs a 5000-way softmax per position.

blocks.question: Which statement about LFQ with 18 latent dimensions is correct?
options: It stores a 262,144 x 256 embedding table and searches it each step
Each token id is an 18-bit number read off the signs of the latent dimensions
It needs the VQ-VAE codebook loss to keep codes from collapsing
Two vectors with the same signs but different magnitudes get different ids
blocks.explain: LFQ quantizes each dimension to sign(z_i) and reads the id as a binary number, so 18 dimensions give 2^18 ids with no table to search. Magnitudes are discarded, and the codebook loss is inapplicable; usage is encouraged by an entropy penalty instead.

blocks.question: FSQ's paper claims near 100 percent codebook usage without auxiliary losses. What is the main reason?
options: The codebook is re-initialised with k-means every epoch
A large commitment weight forces outputs onto codes
Codes are a fixed grid inside a bounded range, so there are no learned codes that can drift away from the data
It uses fewer than 64 codes
blocks.explain: With a bounded encoder output and a fixed rounding grid, every grid cell is a code the encoder can reach. There is no learned code position that can be stranded far from the data, which is what makes VQ codes die.

lessons.title: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion

blocks.md: A tokenizer's output can be measured in bits. Each token is an index into a vocabulary of size K, so it carries at most $\log_2 K$ bits. An image of T tokens therefore stores at most $T \log_2 K$ bits, regardless of how the codes were learned.

blocks.caption: Raw 8-bit RGB versus the token budget. A 256 x 256 image is 196,608 bytes; 256 tokens of 10 bits are 320 bytes.

blocks.title: Bytes per 256 x 256 image, raw versus tokenized

scenes.caption: Raw pixels: 256 x 256 x 3 = 196,608 bytes. Every token budget is a sliver next to it.
Zoom in on tokens only (raw bar set to 0): 320 bytes for VQGAN with 1024 codes (10 bits each), 448 bytes with 16,384 codes (14 bits each), 48 bytes for TiTok's 32 tokens of 12 bits.
As compression ratios: 614.4x, 438.9x and 4096x. A 16x larger vocabulary adds only 4 bits per token, while cutting tokens 8x cuts bits 8x.

blocks.md: Bits are only half the cost. A transformer's attention cost grows roughly with the square of sequence length, so **token count** matters more than vocabulary size for compute: going from 1024 to 256 tokens cuts attention pairs 16x, and from 256 to 32 cuts them 64x. Vocabulary size mostly costs a bigger embedding table and output softmax.

blocks.title: Compression ratio for a 256 x 256 image

scenes.caption: With 10 bits per token (K = 1024) the curve passes through the VQGAN point: 256 tokens give 614.4x.
At 12 bits (K = 4096) the curve passes through TiTok-L-32: 32 tokens give 4096x.
At 18 bits (MAGVIT-v2's 2^18 vocabulary) the ratio drops less than 2x versus 10 bits. Moving along the T axis changes it far more.

blocks.md:
**TiTok** (Yu et al., *An Image is Worth 32 Tokens for Reconstruction and Generation*, 2024) attacks token count. A 2D grid tokenizer ties one token to each image patch, even where neighbouring patches are redundant. TiTok instead appends K learnable **latent tokens** to the ViT encoder's patch tokens and keeps only the latent tokens' outputs, which are then vector-quantized. The decoder, also a ViT, takes the quantized latents plus a grid of mask tokens and reconstructs the image. The token count is therefore set by K, not by the image size.

TiTok-L-32 represents a 256 x 256 image with **32 tokens** from a 4096-entry codebook. With a MaskGIT generator (a masked-token transformer) it reaches 2.77 gFID on ImageNet 256 x 256, versus 6.18 for MaskGIT's own 256-token VQGAN; the paper's best 256 x 256 result, 1.97, uses 128 tokens. At 512 x 512, TiTok-L-64 beat DiT-XL/2 (gFID 2.74 vs 3.04) with 410x faster generation.

TiTok's 32 tokens are not an image patch each. Flattening a 2D grid into a sequence still keeps the grid constraint; a 1D tokenizer lets each token describe any part of the image. Ids from different tokenizers are not interchangeable even at the same length.

**Chameleon** (Meta, 2024) is an *early-fusion* model: images become discrete tokens in the same sequence and vocabulary as text, and one transformer reads and writes both. Its image tokenizer, based on Make-A-Scene (Gafni et al., 2022), encodes a 512 x 512 image into **1024 tokens from a codebook of 8192**. Its BPE vocabulary has 65,536 entries, *including* the 8192 image codes, so an image is just 1024 more ids in the stream. By the formula above that is $1024 \cdot 13 = 13{,}312$ bits against 6,291,456 raw bits, a ratio of about 473.

The Chameleon paper names the cost of this choice: a core weakness of its tokenizer is reconstructing images with a lot of text, which upper-bounds the model on heavy OCR tasks. Whatever the tokenizer drops, no downstream model can recover.

blocks.title: Early fusion: one id stream for text and image

scenes.caption: Text tokens come from the BPE part of the shared 65,536-entry vocabulary.
The image occupies 1024 positions whose ids come from the 8192 image codes in the same vocabulary. One softmax covers both modalities.
Simplified: the marker tokens shown here are illustrative. The model can continue with text after an image, or emit image ids that the tokenizer's decoder renders.

blocks.question: You can either double the codebook from 8192 to 16,384 codes or halve the number of image tokens from 1024 to 512. Which choice reduces the stage 2 transformer's attention compute more, and why?
options: Doubling the codebook, because a larger softmax is the dominant cost
They are equivalent, since both change bits per image by the same factor
Halving tokens, because attention pairs scale with the square of sequence length while codebook size adds only one bit per token
Neither changes compute
blocks.explain: Halving T cuts attention pairs by 4x and bits per image by 2x. Doubling K adds 1 bit per token (13 to 14) and enlarges the embedding and output layers, but leaves sequence length, and thus attention cost, unchanged.

blocks.question: Chameleon's paper says its tokenizer struggles to reconstruct images containing a lot of text. What does that imply for the full model?
options: Nothing, because the transformer can learn the missing detail from more data
Its performance on text-heavy, OCR-like image tasks is upper-bounded by what the tokenizer keeps
Its text-only benchmarks will suffer
It must switch to continuous image features for those inputs
blocks.explain: The transformer only ever sees the token ids. Detail lost at tokenization cannot be recovered downstream, so the tokenizer caps OCR-heavy performance, as the paper states.

blocks.question: TiTok-L-32 and a 16 x 16 VQGAN with 1024 codes both tokenize 256 x 256 images. How many bits per image does each use?
options: 384 bits and 2560 bits
32 bits and 256 bits
4096 bits and 1024 bits
12 bits and 10 bits
blocks.explain: TiTok: 32 tokens x log2(4096) = 32 x 12 = 384 bits. VQGAN: 256 tokens x log2(1024) = 256 x 10 = 2560 bits. TiTok uses about 6.7x fewer bits and 8x fewer tokens.
